title: How to Price a Cake: A Simple Formula for Home Bakers
desc: A step-by-step cake pricing formula for home bakers: ingredients, packaging, your time, overhead and profit margin, with a worked example.
pin: How to price a cake: the simple formula
body:
Most home bakers start by copying what other people charge. The problem is that other people have different ingredient prices, different recipes and different expectations for their own time. A price that works for them can quietly lose you money. This guide gives you a simple formula you can use for every cake, cupcake order or cookie box.

The cake pricing formula

Price = (Ingredients + Packaging + Decorations + Your time + Overhead) ÷ (1 − Profit margin) + Delivery

Each part matters. Leave one out and the cake that looks profitable is actually costing you.

Step 1: Cost the ingredients for this exact cake

Use the recipe you will actually bake, not a rough guess. For each ingredient, divide the package price by the package size to get a cost per gram, cup or piece, then multiply by the amount the recipe uses. Include the things that are easy to forget: butter for greasing, food colouring, vanilla, sprinkles and the second batch of frosting you always end up making.

Step 2: Add packaging and decorations

Cake boards, boxes, cupcake liners, ribbons, toppers, fresh flowers and labels all cost money. Write them down per order. A $3 box on a $40 cake is more than 7% of the price.

Step 3: Pay yourself for your time

This is the line most home bakers skip. Count every hour: shopping, baking, cooling, decorating, cleaning and answering messages. Pick an hourly rate you would accept for skilled work in your area. Even a modest rate changes the picture: three hours at $15 an hour adds $45 to the cost of a cake.

Step 4: Add a share of overhead

Electricity for the oven, baking tools that wear out, your website or Etsy fees, card payment fees and any licence or permit costs are overhead. A simple method is to add up these costs for a month and divide by the number of orders you usually make.

Step 5: Apply your profit margin the right way

Profit is what lets you replace your mixer, invest in new tins and grow. Many bakers add 20–40% on top of costs, but there is a common mistake here. Adding 25% to your cost (a markup) does not give you a 25% margin. To get a true margin, divide by (1 − margin):

  • Cost $78, markup 25% → $78 × 1.25 = $97.50 (your real margin is only 20%)
  • Cost $78, margin 25% → $78 ÷ 0.75 = $104.00 (you keep 25% of the price)

A worked example

ItemAmount
Ingredients$18.00
Packaging (board + box)$4.00
Decorations$6.00
Your time (3 hours × $15)$45.00
Overhead share$5.00
Total cost$78.00
Price at 25% margin ($78 ÷ 0.75)$104.00
Delivery (charged separately)$10.00
Quote to the customer$114.00

Check your price against the market, last

Only after you know your real cost should you look at local prices. If your number is much higher, look for savings in the recipe or the design, or offer a simpler version at a lower price. If your number is lower than the market, you have room to charge more. Avoid simply matching a lower price: you would be paying for your customer's cake.

Make it faster with a calculator

Doing this on paper for every order is slow. A pricing calculator that remembers your ingredient costs and target margin lets you quote in a minute and gives the same answer every time.

title: How to Split Caregiving Costs Fairly Between Siblings
desc: Practical ways to share the cost of caring for an aging parent between brothers and sisters: what counts as a shared cost, fair split methods and how to keep it transparent.
pin: How to split caregiving costs fairly between siblings
body:
Caring for a parent is expensive, and money is one of the most common reasons siblings fall out. Usually it is not because anyone is unfair. It is because nobody wrote down what was paid, who paid it, and what was agreed. A clear, simple system prevents most of those arguments.

Step 1: Agree what counts as a shared cost

Sit down (or video call) and agree on a list. Common shared costs include:

  • Home care aides, respite care and day programs
  • Medication co-pays and medical supplies
  • Mobility aids and home safety changes, such as grab bars or a ramp
  • Transport to appointments
  • Groceries or meal deliveries, if your parent can no longer cover them

Also agree what is not shared, such as your own fuel for a routine visit or a gift you chose to buy. Writing this down once saves a hundred awkward conversations.

Step 2: Choose a split method

There is no single right answer. Families usually choose one of these:

  • Equal shares. Every sibling pays the same percentage. Simple and easy to explain.
  • Income-based shares. Siblings who earn more pay a larger percentage, for example 50 / 30 / 20.
  • Time-adjusted shares. The sibling who provides most of the hands-on care pays a smaller share of costs, because their time is their contribution.

Whatever you choose, write the percentages down and agree to review them every six months or when circumstances change.

Step 3: Log every cost as it happens

For each expense, record the date, what it was, the amount, who paid, and whether it is shared. Keep receipts in one shared folder. Logging as you go is far easier than reconstructing months of spending later.

Step 4: Calculate who owes whom

Once a month, add up all shared costs. Each person's fair share is the total multiplied by their percentage. Compare that to what each person actually paid:

SiblingPaidShareFair shareBalance
Anna$1,34033.3%$722+$618 (is owed)
David$72533.3%$722+$3
Sophie$10233.3%$722−$620 (owes)

Example figures. Total shared costs: $2,167.

A positive balance means that person paid more than their share and is owed money; a negative balance means they owe. In this example, Sophie pays Anna about $618 and the family is level again.

Step 5: Keep it visible to everyone

Transparency is what keeps the peace. Use one shared document that every sibling can open at any time, rather than numbers living in one person's head or in a long group chat. When everyone can see the same figures, the conversation shifts from "who is paying more" to "what does Mom need next".

Talk about the hard parts early

Decide in advance what happens if costs rise sharply, if one sibling cannot pay for a while, or if your parent's own savings should be used first. These are easier to agree on calmly than in a crisis.

title: What to Do in the First 48 Hours After a Parent Dies
desc: A gentle checklist of what needs to happen in the first two days after a death, and what can safely wait until later.
pin: What to do in the first 48 hours after a parent dies
body:
If you are reading this because someone close to you has just died, we are sorry. The first days are overwhelming, and it can feel as if everything must be done at once. It does not. Only a few things truly need to happen in the first 48 hours. Most of the rest can wait a week or longer.

This guide is general information to help you get organised. It is not legal, tax or financial advice. Rules differ between states and countries, so check with a local probate lawyer or the court if you are unsure.

1. Get a legal pronouncement of death

If the death happens in a hospital or care home, staff will usually handle this. If it happens at home and the person was in hospice care, call the hospice. If the death was unexpected, call the emergency number. A pronouncement is needed before the funeral home can take the person into their care and before a death certificate can be issued.

2. Tell close family and friends

Start with the people who need to hear it personally. It is fine to ask one or two others to help pass on the news, so you are not making every call yourself.

3. Arrange care for anyone who depended on them

Children, a spouse who needs support, and pets need someone right away. Make sure they are safe and looked after before anything else.

4. Secure the home and the car

Lock the home, take valuables or important papers somewhere safe, and arrange for someone to collect mail and water plants. An empty home can attract theft, especially if a death notice is published.

5. Look for the will and any funeral wishes

Check for a will, a letter of wishes or a prepaid funeral plan. These may say who the executor is and what kind of funeral the person wanted. Do not distribute any belongings yet, even if family members ask.

6. Contact a funeral home

The funeral home will collect the person, explain your options and usually help you order certified copies of the death certificate. You do not need to decide every detail on the first call.

7. Tell their employer, if they were working

Ask about final pay, any life insurance or death benefits through work, and pension or retirement accounts.

What can wait

  • Closing bank accounts, cancelling subscriptions and notifying most companies
  • Applying to the court or probate office
  • Paying debts or bills from the estate
  • Selling or giving away belongings

These belong to the following weeks. Write them down so you do not need to hold them in your head, and let the first two days be about the person and your family.

A note for executors

If you have been named executor, avoid paying the estate's debts from your own money and keep every receipt for costs you do pay, such as funeral expenses. You may be able to be reimbursed from the estate later.

title: How to Keep a Medication Log for an Aging Parent
desc: What to record in a medication log for an elderly parent, how to track doses and refills, and how to share it with family and doctors.
pin: How to keep a medication log for an aging parent
body:
Older adults often take several medicines, prescribed by different doctors and filled at different times. A single, up-to-date medication log helps everyone involved: the family members who help with doses, the doctor who needs an accurate list, and your parent, who no longer has to remember everything.

This guide is about organisation, not medical advice. Always follow the instructions of your parent's doctor and pharmacist.

What to record for each medicine

  • Name of the medicine and the strength (for example, 20 mg)
  • Form: tablet, capsule, drops, inhaler, patch
  • What it is for, in plain words
  • When it is taken: morning, midday, evening, bedtime, or as needed
  • Who prescribed it, and which pharmacy fills it
  • The next refill date
  • Status: active, or stopped (and the date it was stopped)

Include everything, not only prescriptions

Vitamins, supplements, eye drops, creams and over-the-counter painkillers all belong on the list. Doctors and pharmacists use the full list to check for interactions, so a complete log is more useful than a neat one.

Do not delete stopped medicines

When a medicine is stopped, mark it as stopped instead of deleting the row. A history of what was tried, and when, is often exactly what a new specialist asks for.

Track refills before they run out

Running out of a regular medicine on a weekend is stressful and avoidable. Write the next refill date next to each medicine and check the list once a week. Anything due in the next seven days goes on that week's to-do list, with a name next to it.

Share it with the people who need it

  • Family members who give doses or pick up prescriptions should see the same current list.
  • Doctors: bring a printed copy to every appointment and ask the doctor to confirm it is correct.
  • Emergencies: keep a printed copy with your parent's emergency information, for example on the fridge or in a grab bag.

Review it regularly

Many pharmacists offer medication reviews, and doctors can check whether every medicine is still needed. Bring the log to these conversations. An accurate list makes the review faster and safer.

title: How Much Deposit Should a Home Baker Take for Cake Orders?
desc: How much deposit to ask for custom cake orders, when to ask for it, what to do about cancellations and how to track deposits and balances.
pin: How much deposit should you take for a cake order?
body:
A deposit protects you from the most expensive moment in a home bakery: buying ingredients and blocking out a weekend for an order that is then cancelled. It also tells you the customer is serious. Here is how to set a deposit policy that is fair to you and easy for customers to accept.

A common range: 25% to 50%

Many home bakers ask for between a quarter and half of the order total when the order is confirmed. A simple way to choose:

  • 25–30% for simple, low-cost orders you could easily sell to someone else.
  • 50% for custom designs, large orders, wedding or event cakes and anything with special ingredients or toppers you must buy in advance.
  • 100% upfront for small orders where chasing a balance is not worth the time, or for first-time customers on very busy dates.

At minimum, the deposit should cover the money you spend before baking: ingredients, toppers, boxes and anything ordered specially.

When to ask for it

Ask for the deposit when you confirm the date and the design, and say clearly that the date is only reserved once the deposit is received. This one sentence prevents most double bookings and "maybe" orders.

When the balance is due

Choose one rule and stick to it. Popular options are: balance due a few days before pickup, or balance due at pickup. Asking a few days before gives you time to follow up and means you are not handling payment while a customer is waiting for their cake.

Write a cancellation rule

Customers accept rules they were told about at the start. A simple example: "Deposits are non-refundable within 7 days of the event, because ingredients and decorations are bought in advance. If you cancel earlier, the deposit can be moved to a new date." Check any consumer rules that apply where you live before you finalise your wording.

Track every deposit

As soon as you have more than a few orders a month, it becomes easy to forget who has paid what. For each order, record the total, the deposit requested, the deposit received, the date it arrived and the balance still due. Then, a few days before each pickup, check which balances are still open and send a short reminder.

A short message you can send

Thank you for your order! To reserve your date, a deposit of [AMOUNT] is due by [DATE]. The remaining [BALANCE] is due on [BALANCE DATE]. Once the deposit arrives, I'll confirm your order. Thank you!

title: Executor Checklist: Accounts to Close or Transfer After a Death
desc: A checklist of the accounts an executor usually needs to notify, close or transfer after a death: banks, utilities, subscriptions, insurance, government and online accounts.
pin: Executor checklist: every account to close after a death
body:
One of the longest jobs for an executor is working through every account the person had. Most people have far more than anyone realises. This checklist helps you find them and keep track of each one until it is closed or transferred.

This guide is general information to help you get organised. It is not legal, tax or financial advice. Rules differ between states and countries, so check with a local probate lawyer or the court if you are unsure.

Before you start

  • Get several certified copies of the death certificate. Many organisations need to see one.
  • Have your proof of being executor or administrator ready, once you have it.
  • Gather recent bank statements and the person's mail. Regular payments on a statement are the fastest way to find accounts.

Money and banking

  • Current, checking and savings accounts
  • Credit cards and store cards
  • Loans, mortgages and car finance
  • Investment, brokerage and retirement accounts
  • Safe deposit boxes

Banks usually freeze accounts in the person's sole name once notified. Joint accounts are often treated differently, so ask each bank.

Home and utilities

  • Electricity, gas and water
  • Phone, internet and TV
  • Home insurance (tell the insurer if the home will be empty)
  • Rent or mortgage, property tax

Insurance and pensions

  • Life insurance policies
  • Health and car insurance
  • Pensions and annuities

Government

  • Pension or social security benefits
  • Tax office
  • Passport and driver's licence office
  • Vehicle registration

Subscriptions and memberships

  • Streaming, music and news subscriptions
  • Gym, clubs and charity donations
  • Magazines and delivery services

Online accounts

  • Email accounts
  • Social media: many platforms let you close or memorialise an account
  • Online shopping and payment accounts
  • Cloud storage and photos (ask the family before closing anything with memories)

Track each account to the end

For every account, record the organisation, the account type, the action (close, transfer or keep for now), the date you notified them, whether they asked for a death certificate, and the status. Follow up on anything not confirmed within a few weeks. This record also helps you prepare the final estate statement for the family.

title: Questions to Ask at Your Parent's Doctor Appointment
desc: A practical list of questions to ask when you go with an aging parent to the doctor, plus how to prepare beforehand and what to note afterwards.
pin: Questions to ask at your parent's doctor appointment
body:
Appointments are short, and it is easy to walk out and realise you forgot the one question that mattered. A little preparation turns a rushed ten minutes into a useful conversation.

Before the appointment

  • Write down the main reason for the visit in one sentence.
  • Note any changes since the last visit: new symptoms, falls, sleep, appetite, mood, confusion.
  • Bring the current medication list, including supplements.
  • Agree with your parent which questions they want to ask themselves, and which they would like you to ask.
  • Decide who is driving and who will take notes.

Questions about a new symptom or diagnosis

  • What do you think is causing this?
  • Are there tests we should do, and what will they show?
  • What are the treatment options, and what happens if we wait?
  • What warning signs mean we should call you, or go to urgent care?

Questions about medicines

  • What is this new medicine for, and how will we know it is working?
  • What side effects should we watch for?
  • Does it interact with anything else on the list?
  • Is every medicine on the list still needed?

Questions about daily life

  • Is it safe for my parent to drive, live alone or manage stairs?
  • Is there any equipment or home change that would help?
  • Are there services, therapy or support programs we should look into?

Before you leave

  • Can you summarise the plan in a few sentences?
  • When should we come back, and who do we contact with questions?
  • Will test results be sent to us, or should we call?

After the appointment

Write the notes the same day, while they are fresh: what the doctor said, any medication changes, the next appointment and any follow-ups. Share the notes with the rest of the family so everyone works from the same information.

Respect your parent's voice

Where possible, let your parent speak first and answer for themselves. Your role is to support, remember and fill gaps, not to take over the conversation.

title: How to Calculate Recipe Cost Per Cupcake, Cookie or Slice
desc: Work out the true cost of a recipe per batch and per piece, including small ingredients, waste and packaging, so you can price cupcakes and cookies with confidence.
pin: How to calculate the cost of one cupcake
body:
Knowing the cost of one cupcake, one cookie or one slice is the foundation of every good price. Once you know it, you can price boxes of 6, 12 or 24 in seconds, and spot which products earn you the most.

Step 1: Find the cost per unit of each ingredient

Take the price you paid and divide it by the package size. For example, a 2 kg bag of flour that cost $3.40 costs $0.0017 per gram. A dozen eggs for $4.20 costs $0.35 per egg. Use the same unit the recipe uses: grams, cups, spoons or pieces.

Step 2: Cost the whole batch

Multiply each ingredient's unit cost by the amount in the recipe and add everything together. Do not skip the small things. Vanilla, baking powder, salt and colouring are each tiny, but together they often add 5–10% to a batch.

IngredientAmountUnit costCost
Flour250 g$0.0017 / g$0.43
Sugar200 g$0.0020 / g$0.40
Butter225 g$0.0110 / g$2.48
Eggs4$0.35 each$1.40
Milk, vanilla, baking powder——$0.60
Frosting1 batch—$3.20
Batch total$8.51

Example figures only. Use your own receipts.

Step 3: Divide by the real yield

If the recipe makes 24 cupcakes but one always sticks to the tin and one is a tester, your real yield is 22, not 24. $8.51 ÷ 22 = $0.39 per cupcake in ingredients.

Step 4: Add packaging per piece

Liners, boxes, inserts and labels belong in the cost too. A 12-cupcake box with an insert might cost $1.80, which adds $0.15 per cupcake.

Step 5: Turn cost into a price

Ingredients and packaging are only part of the cost. Add your time and a share of overhead, then apply your profit margin. Our guide on how to price a cake walks through that formula step by step.

Update when prices change

Butter, eggs and chocolate prices move often. Recheck your unit costs every couple of months, or whenever you buy a new package at a different price. When your ingredient list is in a spreadsheet, you update one cell and every recipe updates with it.

title: How Many Death Certificate Copies Do You Need?
desc: Why executors need certified copies of the death certificate, who usually asks for one, and how to estimate how many to order.
pin: How many death certificate copies do you need?
body:
Almost every organisation an executor contacts wants proof of death. Ordering too few copies means waiting weeks for more while accounts stay open. Ordering a sensible number at the start saves time.

This guide is general information to help you get organised. It is not legal, tax or financial advice. Rules differ between states and countries, so check with a local probate lawyer or the court if you are unsure.

Certified copies versus photocopies

Banks, insurers and government offices often ask for a certified copy, issued by the official registry or vital records office, rather than a photocopy. Some will look at a certified copy and return it; others keep it. Ask each organisation which they need before you send one.

Who usually asks for a copy

  • Each bank or building society
  • Each life insurance company and pension provider
  • Investment and retirement account providers
  • The probate court or registry
  • Government benefits and tax offices
  • Vehicle and property registration offices
  • Some utility, phone and credit card companies

How to estimate how many to order

  1. List every bank, insurer, pension and investment provider you know about.
  2. Add one for the court, one for government offices and one or two for property or vehicles.
  3. Add two spare copies for organisations you discover later.

Many families find they need somewhere between a handful and ten or more copies, depending on how many accounts the person had. Copies are usually cheaper to order together at the start than one at a time later, but check the fees where you live.

How to get them

In many places, the funeral home can order copies for you when they register the death. You can usually order more later from the vital records or registry office.

Keep track of every copy

Note who you sent each copy to and whether it will be returned. When an organisation returns a copy, you can reuse it for the next one. A simple documents list, with a status column, prevents copies from disappearing.

title: How to Organize a Care Schedule With Your Family
desc: How to set up a fair caregiving rotation for an elderly parent: mapping care needs, sharing shifts, covering gaps and avoiding burnout.
pin: How to organize a care schedule with your family
body:
When one family member ends up doing nearly all of the care, burnout is only a matter of time. A shared care schedule makes the workload visible and gives everyone a clear part to play, even siblings who live far away.

Step 1: Map what care is actually needed

Write down a normal week: which days and times your parent needs someone present, help with meals or medicines, transport to appointments, shopping, cleaning or company. Separate the tasks that need someone on site from the tasks that can be done from anywhere, such as booking appointments, ordering prescriptions or paying bills.

Step 2: Split the week into shifts

Use simple blocks, such as morning, afternoon, evening and overnight. For each block, decide whether it needs a person present. This makes it much easier to see where the gaps are.

Step 3: Match people to shifts realistically

  • Ask each person what they can genuinely commit to, every week, without resentment.
  • Give remote family members the remote tasks: calls, paperwork, online orders, research.
  • Fill the remaining gaps with paid help, friends, neighbours or community services.

Step 4: Track hours, not only names

Recording the hours each person covers keeps things honest without anyone needing to keep score in their head. If one person's hours keep growing, it is a signal to rebalance before they burn out.

Step 5: Plan for gaps before they happen

Holidays, illness and work trips will happen. Agree on a backup for each regular shift, and keep a short list of people or services you can call at short notice.

Step 6: Hold a short check-in

A fifteen-minute family call every two weeks is enough to review the schedule, share updates from appointments and agree on changes. Keep the schedule, tasks and notes in one shared place so nobody has to search a group chat for information.

Look after the carers too

Build regular time off into the schedule for the main carer. Respite is not a luxury; it is what makes long-term care possible.

title: 8 Customer Message Templates for Home Bakers (Copy and Paste)
desc: Ready-to-use messages for home bakers: first reply, quote, deposit request, order confirmation, reminder, balance due, thank you and review request.
pin: 8 copy-paste messages every home baker needs
body:
Answering customers can take longer than decorating the cake. Saving a set of clear, friendly messages means every customer gets the same information and you stop retyping the same paragraphs. Copy these, add your own voice and keep them somewhere you can reach from your phone.

1. First reply to a new inquiry

Hi [NAME], thank you for getting in touch! To give you a quote, could you tell me the date, how many people it should serve, the flavour you'd like and whether it's pickup or delivery? Photos of designs you like are very welcome.

2. Sending a quote

Thanks for the details! A [SIZE] [FLAVOUR] cake with [DESIGN] would be [PRICE]. Delivery to your area is [DELIVERY FEE]. If you'd like to go ahead, I'll send the deposit details to reserve your date.

3. Deposit request

Lovely! To reserve [DATE], a deposit of [AMOUNT] is due by [DEADLINE]. Your date is confirmed once the deposit arrives. The balance of [BALANCE] is due on [BALANCE DATE].

4. Order confirmation

Your deposit has arrived, thank you! Your order is confirmed: [SUMMARY] for [PICKUP OR DELIVERY] on [DATE] at [TIME]. I'll message you a few days before.

5. Reminder a few days before

Hi [NAME], a quick reminder that your cake is ready for [PICKUP OR DELIVERY] on [DATE] at [TIME]. Please let me know if anything has changed.

6. Balance due

Hi [NAME], the remaining balance of [AMOUNT] for your order is due by [DATE]. You can pay by [METHOD]. Thank you!

7. Thank you after the order

Thank you so much for your order! I hope everyone enjoyed it. It was a pleasure making it for you.

8. Review request

If you have a moment, a short review or a photo tag would mean a lot to my small business. Thank you for supporting a home baker!

Tips for using templates

  • Fill in every bracket before sending. A forgotten [NAME] looks careless.
  • Keep the same order of messages for every customer, so nothing is skipped.
  • Track which stage each order is at: inquiry, confirmed, in production, ready, completed.

title: How to Keep an Estate Ledger as an Executor
desc: Why executors should record every dollar in and out of an estate, what to record, how to handle reimbursements and how a ledger becomes the final statement for beneficiaries.
pin: How to keep an estate ledger as an executor
body:
As executor, you are handling money that belongs to other people: the beneficiaries. The simplest way to protect yourself and keep everyone's trust is to record every payment into and out of the estate, from the first day to the last.

This guide is general information to help you get organised. It is not legal, tax or financial advice. Rules differ between states and countries, so check with a local probate lawyer or the court if you are unsure.

Keep estate money separate

Where possible, open a separate bank account for the estate and run all money through it. Mixing estate money with your own makes the records hard to follow and can cause disputes. Your bank or lawyer can tell you what paperwork is needed to open an estate account where you live.

What to record for every entry

  • Date
  • In or out
  • Category: for example asset sale, refund, funeral, legal fees, property costs, debt payment, distribution
  • Short description
  • Who it was paid to or received from
  • Amount
  • Receipt or reference number

Keep a running balance after each line so you always know how much the estate holds.

Record money you paid personally

Executors and family members often pay early costs, such as the funeral or utility bills, from their own pocket. Record these separately as reimbursements owed, with receipts, and pay them back from the estate once funds are available. Keep a note of the date each one was repaid.

Common entries

Money inMoney out
Bank account balancesFuneral costs
Sale of property, car or belongingsCourt and legal fees
Insurance payouts paid to the estateFinal bills and debts
Refunds from cancelled servicesProperty upkeep and insurance
Final wages or pension paymentsDistributions to beneficiaries

From ledger to final statement

When the work is done, your ledger becomes the estate statement: total received, total paid out, what is left, and what each beneficiary received. Beneficiaries, and in some places the court, may ask to see this. A complete ledger makes this step quick instead of stressful.

Update it weekly

Ten minutes once a week, with receipts in one folder, is far easier than rebuilding months of records at the end.
